chapter_title: From Logic Equations to LUTs: How FPGAs Implement Digital Circuits
chapter_summary:
When you write a digital design in Verilog or VHDL, the FPGA design tool must translate your high-level description into a configuration for the physical FPGA. This process involves several steps: **synthesis**, **technology mapping**, **placement**, and **routing**. Understanding how your logic description maps to FPGA hardware is essential for writing efficient code and debugging timing problems.

**Synthesis** is the process of converting your HDL description into a netlist of primitive logic elements. The synthesis tool reads your Verilog or VHDL code, infers the logic functions, and produces an intermediate representation using generic gates (AND, OR, NOT, flip-flops, multiplexers). For example, if you write `assign Y = (A & B) | (C & D);`, the synthesis tool creates an AND gate for `A & B`, another AND gate for `C & D`, and an OR gate combining them. If you write `always @(posedge clk) Q <= D;`, the synthesis tool infers a D flip-flop.

**Technology mapping** is the process of converting the generic netlist into a netlist of the specific primitives available in the target FPGA. For an Intel FPGA, the target primitives are Logic Elements (LEs), each containing a 4-input LUT, a flip-flop, and a carry chain. The technology mapping tool groups the generic gates into sets that fit into the LUTs and assigns flip-flops to the registers.

For example, consider a 4-input AND function: `Y = A & B & C & D`. This function has four inputs and one output. A 4-input LUT can implement any function of four variables, so the technology mapper places this entire function into a single LUT. The LUT's SRAM cells are programmed with the truth table: the output is 1 only when A=B=C=D=1, and 0 for all other 15 combinations.

Now consider a 5-input AND function: `Y = A & B & C & D & E`. A 4-input LUT can only handle four variables, so the function must be split across two LUTs. The first LUT computes `X = A & B & C & D`, and the second LUT computes `Y = X & E`. This requires two LUTs and one routing connection between them. The technology mapper handles this automatically, but the designer should be aware that wide logic functions consume more LUTs.

For arithmetic operations, the FPGA uses dedicated **carry chains**. A full-adder can be implemented in a single LE: the LUT computes the sum bit, and the dedicated carry logic computes the carry-out using a fast, low-delay path. The carry chain connects adjacent LEs directly, bypassing the general routing network. This is why FPGA adders are much faster than adders built from generic logic gates. When you write `assign sum = a + b;` in Verilog, the synthesis tool recognizes the addition operator and maps it to the carry chain.

For sequential logic, the synthesis tool maps inferred flip-flops to the registers in the CLBs. If you write `always @(posedge clk) q <= d;`, the tool places a D flip-flop in the CLB. The clock signal is connected to the global clock network, which is a specialized, low-skew routing network designed to distribute the clock to all flip-flops simultaneously. The clock enable, reset, and preset signals are also routed through dedicated networks.

The synthesis tool provides reports that show how your design was mapped to the FPGA. The **RTL Viewer** shows the generic netlist before technology mapping, displaying your design as a schematic of gates and flip-flops. The **Technology Map Viewer** shows the netlist after technology mapping, displaying the actual LUTs, flip-flops, and carry chains used. These viewers are powerful debugging tools because they let you verify that the synthesis tool interpreted your HDL code correctly.

screens.title: From Logic Equations to LUTs
screens.subtitle: How HDL becomes configured FPGA resources — LUTs, registers, and carry chains

narration.text: In this chapter you will learn what happens when your Verilog or VHDL description is turned into an FPGA configuration. I will walk you through synthesis, where the tool extracts gates and flip-flops from your code, and technology mapping, where those gates are packed into the device primitives such as 4-input lookup tables and CLB registers. You will see why a four-input function can live in a single LUT but a wider function must be split across multiple LUTs and routing. We will also examine how arithmetic becomes fast with dedicated carry chains and how flip-flops are placed into CLB registers and connected to the clock network. Along the way you will learn to use the RTL Viewer and the Technology Map Viewer to confirm what the tool inferred and how many resources were used. Understanding these mappings helps you write efficient HDL, predict resource use, and diagnose timing problems. By the end you should be able to explain why a 4-bit adder maps differently than a multi-input AND and how synthesis reports reveal that mapping.

keyIdea.title: Why this matters
keyIdea.text: Understanding the synthesis and mapping steps helps you write HDL that uses LUTs, registers, and carry chains efficiently and avoids surprising resource or timing results.

From Logic Equations to LUTs

Follow the path from HDL to gates, then from gates to device primitives. Learn how LUTs, CLB registers, and carry chains implement your design on silicon.

Orientation

You will practice reading synthesis reports and comparing RTL schematic output to the device-specific technology map. This makes it easier to predict LUT count, spot wide logic that must be split, and confirm that inferred flip-flops landed in CLB registers.

In this lesson

Explore Key Topics

How functions fit into N-input LUTs and when split is required.
Carry chains

Viewers

Visual Concept
LUT + FF

Key Takeaway

Synthesis and mapping are distinct steps. Read synthesis reports and use viewers to confirm how your code became LUTs and registers.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you will be able to explain and do after this chapter

narration.text: These objectives show the practical skills you will gain. First, you will explain how a combinational logic function is mapped into a lookup table. That means being able to predict when a function fits in a single LUT and when it must be split. Second, you will describe how flip-flops from your HDL are mapped into registers inside a configurable logic block or CLB. You should be able to point to a flip-flop in the RTL schematic and find the corresponding register in the technology map. Third, you will understand how carry chains implement arithmetic efficiently, why an adder maps differently than generic gates, and how this reduces routing delay. Finally, you will explain the role of synthesis and technology mapping within the FPGA design flow, and use the RTL Viewer and Technology Map Viewer to verify resource usage. Each objective includes an observable checkpoint so you can verify competency: count LUTs for a small function, identify a CLB register, spot a carry chain, and read a mapping report. These skills reduce surprises during synthesis and speed debugging.

keyIdea.title: Verified Competency
keyIdea.text: By practicing these objectives you will predict resource usage and verify the synthesis tool interpreted your HDL as intended.

screens.title: How you will apply these skills
screens.subtitle: Practical checks, reports, and viewer inspections you will perform

narration.text: Beyond definitions, you'll practice measurable checks that show you reached each objective. For LUT mapping, you will synthesize a small combinational function and count the LUTs in the Technology Map Viewer. For flip-flops, you'll write a clocked always block and confirm the inferred D flip-flop became a CLB register in the mapped netlist. For carry chains, you will synthesize a multi-bit adder and observe how each bit uses the carry chain to reduce routing delay. For synthesis and technology mapping, you will open the RTL Viewer to inspect the generic netlist and compare it to the Technology Map Viewer, which shows the actual device primitives. Each activity highlights a common misconception: a wide boolean expression in HDL does not always equal one LUT if inputs exceed the LUT width, and arithmetic operators can map to special hardware rather than generic gates. These hands-on checks give you confidence in reported LUT counts and timing behavior and prepare you to optimize code or request design changes when resources are tight.

keyIdea.title: Practical application
keyIdea.text: Use synthesis and mapping viewers as verification tools that make resource usage and inference visible and actionable.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.3 › How you will apply these skills
Verification checklist
  • Generate a synthesis report and locate the generic netlist in the RTL Viewer.
  • Open the Technology Map Viewer and count LUTs and registers used for a function.
  • Synthesize a 4-bit adder and compare its LUT count to a 4-input AND example.
  • Confirm carries are shown as dedicated chains in the map viewer.
Common misconception

Do not assume a complex expression always fits in one LUT. If the number of distinct inputs exceeds the LUT width, the function will be split across LUTs and require routing between them.

Try this

Synthesize a 5-input AND and observe that two LUTs are used. Then synthesize a 4-input AND and confirm it fits in a single LUT.

screens.title: Synthesis: HDL to Generic Netlist
screens.subtitle: How the tool infers gates and flip-flops from Verilog or VHDL

narration.text: Synthesis reads your HDL and produces a gate-level representation called a generic netlist. The tool recognizes combinational expressions and infers gates such as AND, OR, NOT, multiplexers, and D flip-flops for sequential constructs. For example, the assignment that computes a boolean result from several inputs becomes a small net of gates. A clocked always block with a nonblocking assignment becomes an inferred D flip-flop. Synthesis is not yet tied to the physical device. That comes next. The netlist is useful because it is a human-readable intermediate: you can open the RTL Viewer to see the gates, verify that registers were inferred where you expected, and check that logic was not accidentally inferred as a latch. A common misconception is to think synthesis will optimize away control structure semantics; synthesis preserves functional behavior while optimizing gate count and restructuring logic for efficiency. Practical tip: write clear combinational and sequential constructs so the tool infers the intended gates. Now try a short example: a boolean expression combining AND and OR is synthesized into the corresponding gate network, and a clocked assignment becomes a flip-flop. These are the inputs the mapper uses to allocate LUTs and registers.

keyIdea.title: Synthesis result
keyIdea.text: Synthesis creates a generic netlist of gates and flip-flops that preserves behavior and prepares the design for technology mapping.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.3 › Synthesis: HDL to Generic Netlist
Process

From code to gates

Synthesis infers logic elements and clocked registers without yet considering device primitives. The output is a generic netlist you can inspect.

Example netlist view
// Synthesis inferred gates
// AND gate for A and B
// OR gate combining two ANDs
// D flip-flop inferred from rising-edge block
Misconception
Synthesis preserves behavior; it will not silently change a latch to a flip-flop unless your code signals a clocked transfer.
Pro tip
Write explicit combinational statements and explicit clocked blocks to avoid unintended latches.
Why this matters
  • Netlist shows the actual logical elements the mapper will pack into LUTs.
  • Inspecting the RTL Viewer verifies your HDL was interpreted correctly.
  • Identifies unintended inferred latches or missing registers early.
Key Takeaway

Synthesis creates the intermediate gate-level netlist used by technology mapping to allocate FPGA primitives.

screens.title: Technology Mapping and the 4-input LUT
screens.subtitle: How generic gates become device-specific LUT truth tables

narration.text: Technology mapping takes the generic netlist and fits each function into the primitives available on the target FPGA. In many Intel devices a logic element includes a four-input lookup table and a flip-flop. The mapper decides which group of gates can be implemented as a single LUT truth table. Consider a 4-input AND. All four inputs are distinct, and a 4-input LUT can express any function of those four variables. The mapper writes the LUT SRAM with the truth table so the output is 1 only when all four inputs are 1. This is a literal packing of the boolean function into a table-driven primitive. The key point is that mapping is constrained by the LUT input width. If your boolean function uses more inputs than the LUT supports, the mapper must split the computation across LUTs and insert routing between them. Always inspect the Technology Map Viewer to see which LUTs implement which sub-functions. Being able to read the mapped netlist helps you understand resource consumption and identify candidates for logic restructuring to reduce LUT use. Technology Mapping and the 4-input LUT means a 4-input lut stores a truth table for any function of four variables; mapping groups gates into entries that fit this table.. In practical terms, how generic gates become device-specific lut truth tables. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: LUT as truth table
keyIdea.text: A 4-input LUT stores a truth table for any function of four variables; mapping groups gates into entries that fit this table.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.3 › Technology Mapping and the 4-input LUT
Definition

Mapping netlist to device primitives

The mapper assigns functions to available LUT widths and pairs inferred flip-flops with CLB registers on the device.

4-input AND example
Function: Y = A AND B AND C AND D
Result: Single 4-input LUT programmed with truth table where only A=B=C=D=1 produces 1.
Supporting points
  • Mapper groups gates into sub-functions that fit the LUT input limit.
  • When gates share inputs, they may be packed together to save LUTs.
  • Excess distinct inputs force decomposition across LUTs with routing between them.
Common mistake
Assuming logical equivalence implies equal LUT use. Two logically equivalent forms can map very differently.
Example
A 4-input function maps to one LUT. Adding a fifth distinct input requires a second LUT to combine partial results.

screens.title: Splitting Wide Functions Across LUTs
screens.subtitle: Why a 5-input AND needs more than one LUT and how mappers split logic

narration.text: When a function uses more inputs than a LUT supports, technology mapping decomposes it into smaller sub-functions and chains them with routing. Consider a 5-input AND: the mapper implements X = A AND B AND C AND D in one 4-input LUT and then computes Y = X AND E in a second LUT. This costs two LUTs and one routing net between them. It is important to realize that the mapper chooses sub-functions that minimize overall cost, but the fundamental constraint is LUT width. A common misconception is to assume an optimizer will magically compress many inputs into a single LUT; it cannot because the LUT stores a truth table that has an entry for each input combination. Each LUT can only index up to 2^N entries where N is the LUT width. In practice, grouping inputs that share signals or using intermediate registers can reduce LUT chaining. Understanding this split helps you write HDL that is friendly to mapping or restructure logic into cascades or arithmetic where dedicated hardware exists. Ask yourself: can I restructure the function or infer arithmetic primitives to reduce LUT count?

keyIdea.title: Split logic cost
keyIdea.text: A function wider than the LUT input width is decomposed into multiple LUTs connected by routing; each split adds resource and routing cost.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.3 › Splitting Wide Functions Across LUTs
Scenario

5-input AND decomposition

Mapper chooses X = A & B & C & D in one LUT, then Y = X & E in another. Two LUTs and one routing connection are required.

Concrete example

A logical 5-input AND becomes a short cascade of two LUTs. Each LUT stores truth table entries for its four inputs.

Practical notes
  • Mappers attempt to minimize LUT count but cannot exceed device input width.
  • Chaining increases routing delay compared with a single LUT.
  • Consider sharing intermediate signals or using registers to break logic into stages.
Common mistake

Expecting a single LUT for many-input functions; planning must reflect LUT width limits.

screens.title: Carry Chains: Fast Arithmetic on FPGAs
screens.subtitle: How dedicated carry logic accelerates adders compared with generic gates

narration.text: Carry chains are dedicated, low-latency links between adjacent logic elements that implement the carry propagation in arithmetic operations. When you write an addition expression in Verilog, the synthesis and technology mapping tools recognize the pattern and map each bit of the adder so the LUT computes the sum bit while the carry-out flows through the device's fast carry chain. This direct link bypasses general routing and reduces the critical path for arithmetic, which is why adders are synthesized more efficiently than similar logic composed only of generic gates. A full-adder implementation inside a single logic element illustrates this: the LUT can compute the sum function and the specialized carry logic computes the carry-out quickly. A common contrast is the wide AND chain: without carry hardware, wide arithmetic or multi-bit operations would rely solely on LUTs and general routing, which is slower. Knowing that adders map to carry chains helps you rely on the synthesis tool for arithmetic, while for non-arithmetic multi-input logic you must account for LUT splits. This also explains why a 4-bit adder often uses fewer LUTs than an equivalent logic expression of similar input width.

keyIdea.title: Why adders are fast
keyIdea.text: Dedicated carry chains provide a low-delay path for carry bits, letting each adder bit use one LUT for the sum and the carry logic outside general routing.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.3 › Carry Chains: Fast Arithmetic
Architecture

Dedicated carry logic

Carry chains link adjacent logic elements with low delay so multi-bit adders propagate carries quickly without general routing overhead.

Concrete example

When you write sum = a + b, each bit uses the LUT for sum and the carry chain for carry propagation, yielding faster arithmetic than gate-only implementations.

Why this matters
  • Adders synthesize to fewer LUTs and lower delay because carries use dedicated hardware.
  • Rely on the mapper to detect arithmetic patterns rather than hand-rolling bit-level carries.
  • Compare the technology map of an adder and an equivalent gate netlist to see the difference.
Key Takeaway

Arithmetic uses special carry chains, so writing arithmetic expressions often yields more efficient implementations than composing the same function from generic gates.

screens.title: Flip-Flops, CLB Registers, and Clock Networks
screens.subtitle: How sequential elements from HDL map to physical registers and clocks are distributed

narration.text: Sequential logic is written in HDL as clocked procedures. When the synthesis tool sees a clocked assignment—an always block triggered on a clock edge—it infers a D flip-flop. Technology mapping then assigns that flip-flop to a register inside a configurable logic block. The clock signal that drives these registers is delivered by the FPGA's global clock network, a low-skew specialized routing fabric designed to reach every flip-flop with minimal timing difference. Clock enable, reset, and preset signals are also routed through dedicated resources. Why is this important? Because the placement of registers and the clock distribution affect timing closure. If registers are placed far apart or if their enables require complex routing, you may incur added delay on data or control signals between registers. A common pitfall is assuming that inferred flip-flops will be grouped where you expect; the placer may distribute them to optimize overall routing. Inspecting the Technology Map Viewer confirms which registers correspond to your HDL and helps you reason about clock domain crossing and timing constraints. Flip-Flops, CLB Registers, and Clock Networks means inferred flip-flops become clb registers and rely on the global clock network; verify mapping and placement to avoid timing issues.. In practical terms, how sequential elements from hdl map to physical registers and clocks are distributed. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Registers and clocks
keyIdea.text: Inferred flip-flops become CLB registers and rely on the global clock network; verify mapping and placement to avoid timing issues.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.3 › Flip-Flops, CLB Registers, and Clock Networks
Definition

Sequential mapping

A D flip-flop inferred in HDL is mapped to a register in the CLB. The global clock network distributes the clock to all registers with low skew.

Concrete scenario

You create a rising-edge clocked assignment; the synthesis tool infers a D flip-flop. Mapping assigns it to a CLB register and ties it to the clock network.

Points to check
  • Confirm registers in the Technology Map Viewer match your inferred flip-flops.
  • Verify clock enables and resets are routed through supported dedicated nets.
  • Watch for placement that separates producer and consumer registers, which can create timing pressure.
Pro tip

Use timing reports and the technology map to correlate registers with timing paths and adjust constraints to help the placer.

screens.title: RTL Viewer vs Technology Map Viewer
screens.subtitle: Use both viewers to understand synthesis interpretation and device mapping

narration.text: The RTL Viewer and the Technology Map Viewer show two different stages in the flow. The RTL Viewer shows the generic netlist produced by synthesis: gates, inferred flip-flops, and the logical structure of your design. The Technology Map Viewer shows the result after mapping: LUT instances, assigned flip-flops in CLBs, and carry chain connections. Use the RTL view to confirm that behavioral constructs became the gates you expect. Use the Technology Map view to confirm how those gates were packed into LUTs and where carry chains or registers appear. A practical workflow is to find a suspicious timing path in the timing report, open the RTL Viewer to identify the high-level gates involved, then open the Technology Map Viewer to see how those gates were laid out in hardware. This two-step inspection helps you verify tool interpretation and focus optimization efforts where mapping produced inefficient use of LUTs or introduced long routing nets. Always cross-check both viewers when resource counts or timing differ from your expectations. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Two complementary views
keyIdea.text: RTL Viewer = logical netlist; Technology Map Viewer = device primitive mapping. Use both to verify behavior and resource use.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.3 › RTL Viewer vs Technology Map Viewer
RTL Viewer
Shows the generic netlist from synthesis: gates, multiplexers, and inferred flip-flops. Useful for verifying how HDL was interpreted.
Use case
Confirm registers and check for unintended latches or incorrect behavioral inference.
Technology Map Viewer
Shows actual LUT instances, CLB registers, and carry chains after mapping to device primitives.
Use case
Count LUTs, identify carry chains, and verify register placement for timing analysis.
Workflow tip

If timing or resource counts surprise you, locate the path in a timing report, inspect the RTL netlist to find the logical source, then open the Technology Map Viewer to see the mapped LUTs and registers to guide optimization.

screens.title: Estimating LUT Count: 6-input AND Example
screens.subtitle: Walkthrough: how many 4-input LUTs does a 6-input AND need?

narration.text: Estimating resource use helps set expectations before synthesis. For a 6-input AND you must decompose the function to fit 4-input LUTs. One straightforward decomposition computes X = A AND B AND C AND D in the first LUT, then computes Y = X AND E AND F in the second. Each LUT takes up to four inputs: the second LUT uses X plus E and F and may leave one LUT input unused. This requires at least two LUTs. The synthesis tool may choose different groupings but cannot implement six distinct inputs in a single 4-input LUT. This simple example also highlights why arithmetic uses fewer LUTs: a 4-bit adder uses dedicated carry chains so each bit typically uses one LUT for the sum and the carry is handled by the chain. When you compare a 6-input AND to a 4-bit adder, the adder benefits from carry hardware and tends to be more resource-efficient. Use this reasoning to answer assessment questions and to estimate LUT counts before you run synthesis. Verify by synthesizing the functions and checking the Technology Map Viewer.

keyIdea.title: Estimation rule
keyIdea.text: A function with more distinct inputs than the LUT width must be implemented with multiple LUTs; a 6-input AND requires at least two 4-input LUTs.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.3 › Estimating LUT Count: 6-input AND
Step-by-step estimate
  1. Identify distinct inputs: A, B, C, D, E, F. That's six inputs.
  2. Map up to four inputs into one LUT: compute X = A AND B AND C AND D.
  3. Use a second LUT for Y = X AND E AND F. Total at least two LUTs.
Assessment idea

Ask: How many 4-input LUTs are needed for a 6-input AND? Answer: At least two.

Compare with adder

A 4-bit adder often maps to one LUT per bit for sum with carry handled by the carry chain, so the adder can use fewer LUTs than a similarly wide gate-only expression.

Key Takeaway

Estimate resource use by counting distinct inputs and knowing the LUT width; verify with the Technology Map Viewer.

screens.title: Placement and Routing: Why Mapping Isn't the Whole Story
screens.subtitle: How placement and routing affect timing after mapping to LUTs and registers

narration.text: After technology mapping allocates LUTs and registers, placement and routing determine the physical locations and interconnections on the device. Placement assigns each LUT and register to specific logic elements or CLBs; routing connects nets between them across the programmable fabric. Even if mapping packs logic well, poor placement or long routing paths can introduce timing problems. For example, two LUTs connected by a routed net that spans many interconnect resources may slow a critical path. The design flow therefore includes placement and routing steps that attempt to minimize delay while respecting constraints and device resources. You should use synthesis reports, timing analysis, and the Technology Map Viewer together: mapping shows which primitives are used, while post-placement timing reports reveal whether those primitives meet timing once placed and routed. If timing fails, consider logic restructuring, changing constraints, or using pipeline registers to break long paths. This step completes the translation from HDL to a routable configuration and is essential to achieving a working, timing-closed design. keyIdea.title: Placement & routing matter
keyIdea.text: Mapping defines resources; placement and routing determine whether those resources meet timing and connectivity requirements on chip.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.3 › Placement and Routing
What happens next

Placement assigns mapped LUTs and registers to physical CLBs; routing connects nets. These steps affect timing even after mapping looks correct.

Practical checks
  • Run post-route timing analysis to find critical nets introduced by routing.
  • Inspect placed instances in the technology map to see physical grouping.
  • Consider pipelining or constraints when routing delay is too high.
Why this matters

Even an optimal mapping can fail timing if placement scatters critical path elements or routing uses long nets. Mapping is necessary but not sufficient for timing closure.

Common mistake

Assuming mapped LUT count guarantees timing. Only post-placement timing reports confirm critical path delays after routing.

screens.title: Synthesis Lab: 4-bit Comparator and Resource Counting
screens.subtitle: Guided steps to synthesize, view, and count LUTs and flip-flops

narration.text: This hands-on activity reinforces the mapping concepts. Implement a 4-bit magnitude comparator in Verilog that compares two 4-bit inputs and outputs greater-than, equal, and less-than signals. Synthesize it for the target device and open the RTL Viewer to inspect the generic netlist and check inferred gates and flip-flops. Then open the Technology Map Viewer to count how many LUTs and registers were used. Compare those counts to a 4-bit adder synthesized for the same device. You should observe that the adder benefits from carry chains and may use fewer routing resources than a comparable comparator built from generic gates. Document how many LUTs and flip-flops each design uses. A common pitfall when doing this lab is forgetting to add explicit registers if you intended registered outputs; the synthesis tool will infer combinational logic instead. Record screenshots of both viewers and note any places where logic was split across LUTs. This exercise trains you to verify mapping results and to connect HDL style choices to resource outcomes. keyIdea.text: Synthesize a 4-bit comparator, inspect RTL and Technology Map viewers, and compare LUT/register counts to a 4-bit adder to see mapping differences.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.3 › Synthesis Lab: 4-bit Comparator
Steps
  1. Write a Verilog module that outputs A>B, A==B, and A<B for 4-bit inputs.
  2. Synthesize for your target device and open the RTL Viewer to inspect inferred gates and registers.
  3. Open the Technology Map Viewer and count LUTs and flip-flops used.
  4. Synthesize a 4-bit adder and compare resource usage and presence of carry chains.
Checklist

  • Capture screenshots of both viewers documenting LUT counts.
Key Takeaway

Hands-on synthesis and viewer inspection is the fastest way to connect HDL style to mapped hardware resources.

screens.title: Practical Tips to Influence Mapping
screens.subtitle: Simple HDL patterns and restructuring that can reduce LUT use or routing cost

narration.text: You can influence how synthesis and mapping treat your design by making small code or structural choices. First, use arithmetic operators where appropriate. The synthesis tool recognizes addition and subtraction patterns and maps them to carry chains, which reduces LUT and routing load compared with hand-rolled logic. Second, reduce distinct input counts for wide boolean functions by factoring shared terms or reusing intermediate signals so more logic fits inside single LUTs. Third, add pipeline registers to break long combinational paths, which reduces routing pressure and helps timing closure. Fourth, write explicit combinational blocks for pure logic and explicit clocked blocks for registers to avoid accidental latches. Fifth, when a function must be wide, consider restructuring into stages or using a small tree of LUTs with registered intermediates. These practices do not change functionality, but they give the mapper more opportunities to pack or accelerate logic. A common misconception is that the tool will always find the optimal packing; in complex designs, small rewrites often produce measurable resource or timing improvements. screens.title: Key Concepts: What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Concise reminders of the mapping flow and resource behavior

narration.text: Let's recap the essential points to remember. First, synthesis converts HDL into a generic netlist of gates and inferred flip-flops. Second, technology mapping fits those gates into device primitives — LUTs and CLB registers — and is constrained by LUT input width. Third, carry chains are dedicated hardware that make arithmetic fast and more resource-efficient than gate-only implementations. Fourth, inferred flip-flops are assigned to CLB registers and driven by the global clock network, so placement and clock routing affect timing. Fifth, use the RTL Viewer to inspect the logical netlist and the Technology Map Viewer to confirm mapped instances, LUT counts, and presence of carry chains. These quick reminders tie the chapter together and give you a checklist for diagnosing resource or timing surprises in your FPGA designs.
